title: Introduce lint probing tiers and release holden-window orchestrator
author: Leah Chen
description: Motivation: Our presubmit feedback tail is dominated by noisy lint jobs that run identical checks across every changed package. This patch introduces 'lint probing tiers' to quickly sample change impact and route full lint to targeted lanes only when probing detects risk. In parallel, we add a release 'holden-window' orchestrator to provide a quieting period around releases where non-critical lint churn is throttled and release-smoke jobs are prioritized. Implementation summary: 1) Tiered presubmit lanes: probe-fast, probe-deep, full-lint. probe-fast runs a focused rule subset and file-change heuristics. probe-deep adds a broader rule set and an adaptive timeout. full-lint is reserved for failures or explicitly labeled PRs. 2) Routing service: small Golang lambda (ci/router) added that inspects changed-files, cache hints, and recent infra failures to choose the lane. 3) Release holden-window: a lightweight coordinator (ci/release-holden) that sets ephemeral repo labels and adjusts merge gates for a configurable window (defaults: 30m pre-release to 90m post-release). During holden windows, low-risk probe results may be queued, high-priority smoke and canary jobs are bumped. 4) Local dev flow: 'rwlint' dev shim added to replicate probe behavior locally. 5) Migration: existing presubmit workflow now delegates to the router via a single action; older monolithic lint jobs were decomposed into per-language actions. Rollout plan: staged rollout to main: enable probe-fast on draft PRs for one week, opt-in probe-deep on 10% of PRs week two, flip default routing week three and enable holden-window for each release pipeline. Backout: router includes a feature flag (CI_ROUTER_MODE=legacy) to restore previous behavior; holden-window can be disabled per release by passing release.holden=false. Testing: unit tests for router decision matrix, e2e runs in the perf-canary org, manual verification across redwood and redwood-docs repos. Observability: added Prometheus counters (lint_probe_decisions, holden_window_active_seconds) and a Grafana panel in CI dashboard showing lane distribution and holden window events. Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked (ENG-2314) - [x] Router and orchestrator unit tests - [x] Integration tests against presubmit-sandbox - [x] rwlint local shim and README - [x] Observability dashboard and alerts - [x] Migration plan + feature flag Comments on UX: aim to reduce median presubmit time by routing non-risky PRs away from full-lint; developers can request full-lint by adding 'ci:full-lint' label. Security considerations: the router only reads PR metadata and changed files; it does not run arbitrary code. The holden orchestrator requires repo-level label write permissions; deployment uses existing CI service accounts and audit logs are enabled.

review_conversation: Marco: Can we opt new repos in selectively? Author: Yes, router respects a repo opt-in list (ci.config). Marco: Add metric for lane rejections. release_notes: Introduce tiered lint probing to speed presubmit feedback and a release 'holden-window' to reduce churn around releases. Adds router/orchestrator services, local rwlint shim, and observability. Rollout is staged and feature-flagged.
notes_for_release_manager: Default holden-window: 30m pre to 90m post. To disable for a release set release.holden=false in release-job. Monitor Grafana panel 'CI - Lint Lanes' and alert on lane-rejection-rate > 5%.
migration_steps: 1) Deploy router and orchestrator behind feature flag. 2) Update .github workflows to delegate to lane-delegator. 3) Opt repos via ci.config for gradual coverage. 4) Monitor metrics for 72h before flipping default. 5) Remove legacy monolithic-lint job after 2 weeks of stable metrics.
postmerge_tasks: create a task to add Slack notify for holden-window activation, follow up PR to add Go-based lane simulator for load testing, communicate change in #dev-ci channel
user_impact: Short-term: some PRs may change presubmit timing as they get routed to probe lanes. Long-term: faster median feedback and fewer wasted full-lint runs.
